# The Lost Art of Drifting

In the last year, I have been trying to learn how to do nothing again. Not the performative nothing of a meditation app, with its timed bells and guided breathing, but the older, shabbier nothing of sitting on a front step and watching the light change. It is harder than it sounds. The moment I sit still, my hand twitches toward my phone, my mind starts composing a list, and I feel a small electric guilt about all the things I should be doing. This, I have come to believe, is one of the quiet tragedies of modern life: we have forgotten how to drift.

Drifting used to be a natural human state. A child lying in the grass, staring at clouds, is drifting. A teenager walking home the long way, listening to music, is drifting. A person staring out a bus window at a city they have seen a thousand times is drifting. It is a state of open attention, neither focused nor absent, where thoughts are allowed to move at their own pace, bumping into each other, forming unexpected connections. It is not productive. It does not generate data. It cannot be optimized. And yet it is in these moments that we often feel most like ourselves.

What replaced drifting is a culture of continuous optimization. We carry devices that measure our steps, our sleep, our heartbeats, our screen time. We listen to podcasts at double speed while doing the dishes. We turn our hobbies into side hustles and our vacations into photo content. Even our rest is scheduled, labeled, and quantified. The message, repeated everywhere, is that time must be used, not simply inhabited. But there is a cost to this way of living. When every moment is directed toward an outcome, we lose the capacity for the kind of aimless awareness that feeds the imagination.

I first noticed this in myself on a long train ride. I had no Wi-Fi, no signal, no book. For the first hour, I was restless. I checked my phone repeatedly, even though there was nothing to check. I felt a vague anxiety, as if I were missing something important. But after a while, something shifted. I began to notice the landscape outside the window. Not just see it, but actually notice it—the way the light fell on a distant field, the arrangement of roofs in a small town, the slow curve of a river. My thoughts slowed down. I remembered a conversation I’d had years ago, a dream from the night before, an idea for a story I’d never written. By the time the train arrived, I felt strangely refreshed, as if I had finally given my mind room to breathe.

That experience taught me something important: our attention is not a machine. It is a living thing, and like any living thing, it needs both focus and fallow time. Focus is important, of course. We need to be able to concentrate on difficult tasks, to push through boredom, to work with intention. But focus without rest becomes brittle. It narrows our perception and makes us rigid. Drifting, on the other hand, restores a wider view. It allows us to see connections that focused attention misses. It is the difference between staring at a map and wandering through a landscape. The map is useful, but it cannot tell you how the air smells after rain.

Many creative people have understood this intuitively. The poet Mary Oliver wrote about the importance of idleness, of walking in the woods with no particular destination. The philosopher Bertrand Russell praised “fruitful monotony,” the kind of repetitive, undemanding activity that lets the mind wander. Scientists like Einstein and Poincaré reported that some of their best insights came not during focused work, but during moments of mental relaxation—while shaving, walking, or staring out a window. When we stop forcing our attention toward a single goal, the brain’s default mode network becomes more active. This network is associated with daydreaming, memory, and associative thinking. In other words, drifting is not a waste of time; it is a form of cognitive maintenance.

And yet we resist it, because drifting is uncomfortable. When we drift, we are left alone with our thoughts, and our thoughts are not always pleasant. They drift toward our regrets, our fears, our unanswered questions. In a world where we can always find a distraction, it takes courage to sit with the static of our own minds. But this is precisely why drifting is so valuable. It is a way of making peace with ourselves, of learning to tolerate the full range of our inner experience, not just the pleasant parts.

There is also a social dimension to our loss of drifting. When we are always busy, always optimized, always available, we have less time for the kind of unstructured socializing that used to bind communities together. The long afternoon visit, the impromptu walk, the conversation that starts about nothing and ends somewhere unexpected—these are becoming rare. In their place, we have scheduled meetups, video calls with agendas, and text exchanges that are efficient but often hollow. Drifting, in this sense, is not just a personal practice; it is a social one. It is the space in which intimacy grows.

So how do we reclaim drifting? I do not think it requires dramatic changes. It does not mean abandoning technology or moving to a cabin in the woods. It means making small, deliberate choices to leave some time unstructured. It means walking without a podcast, sitting on a park bench without a purpose, staring out a window without reaching for a phone. It means allowing ourselves to be bored, and then discovering that boredom is not an emptiness to be filled but a doorway to a richer kind of attention.

The more I practice this, the more I notice the texture of the world. The way the light changes on the kitchen wall in the late afternoon. The sound of rain on the roof at night. The particular silence of a city street just before dawn. These are not spectacular things. They are not experiences that can be filmed or shared or turned into a story. They are simply there, waiting to be noticed. And in noticing them, I feel less like a machine and more like a human being.

I think often of a line from Wallace Stevens: “Perhaps the truth depends on a walk around the lake.” I did not understand it for a long time. But now I think I do. The truth is not always something to be pursued directly. Sometimes it emerges when we stop pursuing, when we allow our attention to soften and wander. The truth depends on a walk around the lake because the truth is not a destination; it is a way of seeing. And seeing requires time—unhurried, aimless, drifting time.

So I will keep practicing. I will keep leaving gaps in my day, even though the world tells me to fill them. I will keep walking, not to get somewhere, but to be somewhere. And I will keep watching the light change, knowing that in that small act of attention, I am doing something important. I am learning, again, how to be alive.

The Lost Art of Drifting

In the last year, I have been trying to learn how to do nothing again. Not the performative nothing of a meditation app, with its timed bells and guided breathing, but the older, shabbier nothing of sitting on a front step and watching the light change. It is harder than it sounds. The moment I sit still, my hand twitches toward my phone, my mind starts composing a list, and I feel a small electric guilt about all the things I should be doing. This, I have come to believe, is one of the quiet tragedies of modern life: we have forgotten how to drift.

Drifting used to be a natural human state. A child lying in the grass, staring at clouds, is drifting. A teenager walking home the long way is drifting. A person staring out a bus window at a city they have seen a thousand times is drifting. It is a state of open attention, neither focused nor absent, where thoughts are allowed to move at their own pace, bumping into each other, forming unexpected connections. It is not productive. It does not generate data. It cannot be optimized. And yet it is in these moments that we often feel most like ourselves.

What replaced drifting is a culture of continuous optimization. We carry devices that measure our steps, our sleep, our heartbeats, our screen time. We listen to podcasts at double speed while doing the dishes. We turn our hobbies into side hustles and our vacations into photo content. Even our rest is scheduled, labeled, and quantified. The message, repeated everywhere, is that time must be used, not simply inhabited. But there is a cost. When every moment is directed toward an outcome, we lose the capacity for the kind of aimless awareness that feeds the imagination.

I first noticed this in myself on a long train ride. I had no Wi-Fi, no signal, no book. For the first hour, I was restless. I checked my phone repeatedly, even though there was nothing to check. I felt a vague anxiety, as if I were missing something important. But after a while, something shifted. I began to notice the landscape outside the window. Not just see it, but actually notice it—the way the light fell on a distant field, the arrangement of roofs in a small town, the slow curve of a river. My thoughts slowed down. I remembered a conversation I’d had years ago, a dream from the night before, an idea for a story I’d never written. By the time the train arrived, I felt strangely refreshed, as if I had finally given my mind room to breathe.

That experience taught me something important: our attention is not a machine. It is a living thing, and like any living thing, it needs both focus and fallow time. Focus is important, of course. We need to be able to concentrate on difficult tasks, to push through boredom, to work with intention. But focus without rest becomes brittle. It narrows our perception and makes us rigid. Drifting, on the other hand, restores a wider view. It allows us to see connections that focused attention misses. It is the difference between staring at a map and wandering through a landscape. The map is useful, but it cannot tell you how the air smells after rain.

Many creative people have understood this intuitively. Mary Oliver wrote about the importance of idleness, of walking in the woods with no particular destination. Bertrand Russell praised “fruitful monotony,” the kind of repetitive, undemanding activity that lets the mind wander. Scientists like Einstein and Poincaré reported that some of their best insights came not during focused work, but during moments of mental relaxation—while shaving, walking, or staring out a window. When we stop forcing our attention toward a single goal, the brain’s default mode network becomes more active. This network is associated with daydreaming, memory, and associative thinking. Drifting is not a waste of time; it is a form of cognitive maintenance.

And yet we resist it, because drifting is uncomfortable. When we drift, we are left alone with our thoughts, and our thoughts are not always pleasant. They drift toward our regrets, our fears, our unanswered questions. In a world where we can always find a distraction, it takes courage to sit with the static of our own minds. But this is precisely why drifting is so valuable. It is a way of making peace with ourselves, of learning to tolerate the full range of our inner experience, not just the pleasant parts.

There is also a social dimension to our loss of drifting. When we are always busy, always optimized, always available, we have less time for the kind of unstructured socializing that used to bind communities together. The long afternoon visit, the impromptu walk, the conversation that starts about nothing and ends somewhere unexpected—these are becoming rare. In their place, we have scheduled meetups, video calls with agendas, and text exchanges that are efficient but often hollow. Drifting, in this sense, is not just a personal practice; it is a social one. It is the space in which intimacy grows.

So how do we reclaim drifting? I do not think it requires dramatic changes. It does not mean abandoning technology or moving to a cabin in the woods. It means making small, deliberate choices to leave some time unstructured. It means walking without a podcast, sitting on a park bench without a purpose, staring out a window without reaching for a phone. It means allowing ourselves to be bored, and then discovering that boredom is not an emptiness to be filled but a doorway to a richer kind of attention.

The more I practice this, the more I notice the texture of the world. The way the light changes on the kitchen wall in the late afternoon. The sound of rain on the roof at night. The particular silence of a city street just before dawn. These are not spectacular things. They are not experiences that can be filmed or shared or turned into a story. They are simply there, waiting to be noticed. And in noticing them, I feel less like a machine and more like a human being.

I think often of a line from Wallace Stevens: “Perhaps the truth depends on a walk around the lake.” I did not understand it for a long time. But now I think I do. The truth is not always something to be pursued directly. Sometimes it emerges when we stop pursuing, when we allow our attention to soften and wander. The truth depends on a walk around the lake because the truth is not a destination; it is a way of seeing. And seeing requires time—unhurried, aimless, drifting time.

So I will keep practicing. I will keep leaving gaps in my day, even though the world tells me to fill them. I will keep walking, not to get somewhere, but to be somewhere. And I will keep watching the light change, knowing that in that small act of attention, I am doing something important. I am learning, again, how to be alive.
